Stated Claim / Post Context:
Introducing my undesirable friends

The second part of Julia Loktev’s documentary epic follows its Russian journalists into exile

Actual Article Body:
The last time filmgoers saw the female journalists of TV Rain, Russia’s sole remaining independent news channel, they were dashing to the airport. Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow had spent five-and-a-half hours documenting their efforts to call Vladimir Putin and his apparatchiks to account. They logged example after example of state corruption, censorship and misinformation. In return, they were labelled “foreign agents”. Then, on 24th February 2022, Russia launched its fullscale invasion of Ukraine. TV Rain’s reporters and editors knew that, if they stayed in the country, they would almost certainly be jailed.

Now, in My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, Loktev shows the women scattered across Europe and beyond, trying to pick up the pieces. Their bank accounts have been frozen. They’re separated from their loved ones. If they return to Russia, even to visit a sick parent, they risk arrest. One likens their psychological state to Valhalla—a “supposed paradise that actually is hell. You’re in this endless loop of time when you’re thinking only about the past, remembering your past exploits. And it’s very hard to overcome this feeling of life after death.”

Undimmed, for the most part, is their belief in the importance of holding Putin to account. They set up podcasts, private Telegram groups for the friends and families of political prisoners, alternative media archives. TV Rain itself is resurrected in a borrowed studio in the Latvian capital, Riga. They make ingenious use of anonymous cameramen and wedding videographers to capture damning footage. Many Ukrainians, though, refuse to talk to them; they’re seen as Russians, guilty by birth. Moscow, meanwhile, dubs them traitors and tries them in absentia. Mourns one: “You feel like it’s 1941 and you’re simultaneously the German and the Jew.”

They work tirelessly, glue themselves to their screens, chase leads around the clock. Yet, inevitably, they have doubts. If presenting the truth is so vital, why is Rashism—the term, popularised in Ukraine, for Putin’s brand of fascism—still in the ascendant? Are they preaching to the converted or do they offer hope to those Russians who pine for better? How should they talk about their countrymen: is a drafted soldier fundamentally an occupier or does he deserve empathy?
